title: Root Canals for Children: Baby Teeth, Pulpotomies, and When They're Needed
metaTitle: Root Canals for Children: Baby Teeth & Pulpotomies
metaDescription: Do children ever need root canals on baby teeth? Learn about pulpotomies and pulpectomies, why saving primary teeth matters, and how kids' treatment differs.
excerpt: Yes, children sometimes need root canal-type treatment on baby teeth. Here is what a pulpotomy and pulpectomy involve, why saving primary teeth matters, and how it differs from adult care.
heroImageAlt: A young child smiling comfortably at a friendly, family-oriented dental visit.
bodyHtml:
Do children ever need a root canal on a baby tooth?

Yes — children sometimes need root canal-type treatment on baby (primary) teeth when decay or injury reaches the pulp inside the tooth. In children, this is usually done as a pulpotomy or a pulpectomy rather than the full adult root canal procedure, and the goal is to relieve pain, treat infection, and keep the natural baby tooth in place until it is ready to fall out on its own. Although it can be surprising to hear that a tooth destined to be lost anyway is worth saving, primary teeth do important work, and keeping them healthy often matters more than parents expect.

Why saving a baby tooth matters

Baby teeth are not just placeholders to be ignored. They help children chew and eat comfortably, support clear speech, and — importantly — hold space in the jaw for the adult teeth developing underneath. If a baby tooth is lost too early to decay or infection, neighbouring teeth can drift into the gap, which may crowd or complicate how the permanent teeth come in. Treating an infected baby tooth can also prevent pain and the spread of infection. For these reasons, dentists often recommend trying to save a primary tooth where it is reasonable to do so.

Pulpotomy vs pulpectomy: the two main approaches

These terms describe how much of the pulp tissue is treated:

  • Pulpotomy. When decay or inflammation affects the upper portion of the pulp (inside the crown of the tooth) but the roots are still healthy, the dentist removes the affected pulp from the crown, treats the area, and places a medicated material to calm and protect what remains. The tooth is then restored, often with a crown designed for children.
  • Pulpectomy. When infection extends further into the root canals of a baby tooth, more of the pulp tissue is removed, similar in principle to an adult root canal but adapted for primary teeth. The canals are cleaned and filled with a material that the body can resorb as the baby tooth naturally loosens.

The right approach depends on how far the problem has progressed, which a dentist assesses with an examination and X-rays.

How children's treatment differs from adults'

Primary teeth have different anatomy and a limited lifespan, so the materials and techniques are tailored to them — for example, fillings in a pulpectomy are designed to break down as the root naturally dissolves ahead of the tooth falling out. Just as important is the child's experience. Dentists who treat children focus on a gentle, reassuring approach, clear and age-appropriate explanations, and keeping the visit as calm as possible. The tooth is numbed for comfort, as it would be for an adult.

Will my child be in pain?

The treatment is carried out with the tooth numbed, so your child should not feel sharp pain during the procedure. In fact, these treatments are often done precisely to relieve the pain of an infected or inflamed tooth. Mild tenderness afterward is usually manageable, and your dentist will advise on comfort and aftercare.

Is it better to just pull the baby tooth?

Not always. Because baby teeth hold space for adult teeth and support chewing and speech, keeping a treatable tooth is often preferable to removing it early. That said, extraction is sometimes the right choice depending on the tooth and the situation. Your dentist can explain the trade-offs for your child specifically.

How do I keep it from happening again?

Good daily brushing, a tooth-friendly diet, and regular dental check-ups help catch small problems before they reach the pulp. Early, routine visits also help children feel comfortable at the dentist over time.

Family-friendly care in Markham

If your child has a toothache, a visible cavity, or an injured tooth, an early check-up is the right next step so a dentist can decide whether treatment is needed.
